1) FV is an indispensable clot‐promoting protein that is required for normal platelet function, 2) FV is required for the formation of a platelet plug and 3) FV is also required for the formation and stabilization of the fibrin clot.

FV deficiency in humans is not uniformly fatal, that the bleeding tendency is not only dependent on FV level, but also on the interaction of FV with platelets, and that the prothrombotic tendency of FV deficiency is dependent on FV plasma levels and the presence of tissue factor pathway inhibitors in plasma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of mechanisms underlying the variable bleeding phenotype in FV deficiency and the development of new treatment strategies.
the molecular and cellular basis of FV deficiency, and with the identification of novel treatment strategies for FV‐deficiency.
the identification of the mechanisms that protect FV‐defective patients from severe bleeding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FV deficiency is a complex bleeding disorder, which can be best described by a combination of quantitative and qualitative platelet dysfunction, as well as a reduced anticoagulant capacity.
FV is a key factor in haemostasis and that its deficiency is associated with a variable bleeding tendency that is influenced by the interplay of several factors.
FV deficiency is a bleeding diathesis, which is not necessarily severe, but can be life‐threatening in newborns and in patients undergoing invasive procedures or suffering from trauma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the bleeding tendency in FV deficiency is determined not only by the severity of the deficiency, but also by the interaction between the plasma FV levels and the function of the platelets, and that the risk of bleeding can be further influenced by the presence of other risk factors such as a history of previous haemorrhage and/or the concomitant use of antithrombotic drugs.

FV deficiency is a heterogeneous bleeding disorder, with a variable clinical expression that is determined not only by the plasma levels of FV but also by platelet function and the balance between pro‐ and anticoagulant factors in plasma.

FV deficiency is not as simple as one might think, but that it is a complex disease, in which platelets, the coagulation factor FVIII and the anticoagulant tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) play a crucial role in determining the clinical phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
platelet function is crucial in the bleeding diatheses of FV deficiency, and this is particularly important in the neonatal period, as well as in the setting of trauma and surgery.

platelets and plasma TF pathway inhibitor are important players in the haemostatic defect of FV deficiency and that the severity of bleeding is determined by the combined effects of these and possibly other mechanisms.
FV deficiency is not simply a quantitative defect of FV, but rather a complex disease in which platelets and other factors play a major role.
